primarySense: similar in a way that permits a meaningful comparison

nearSynonyms.difference: exactly the same; analogous is similar in structure or function
uniform throughout, not comparable across

examples.text: A bird's wing and a butterfly's wing are analogous: both enable flight, but they evolved separately from different structures.
The economist argued that a national budget is not analogous to a family budget, since governments can print money.
The collapse of the Soviet Union was, in some ways, analogous to the fall of Rome: both empires crumbled from within.

satPassage: Neuroscientists often compare memory formation to the way a path forms in a field: the more often a route is walked, the clearer it becomes. Similarly, repeated use strengthens connections between neurons, making the two processes ____ in a useful way.

primarySense: fundamentally different and distinct in kind

nearSynonyms.difference: varied, often positively; disparate stresses incompatible difference
separate and distinct, not necessarily different in kind

confusables.note: desperate = hopeless or in great need

examples.text: The coalition united disparate groups—farmers, students, and factory owners—who agreed on little else.
The historian wove together disparate sources, from tax records to love poems, into a single narrative.
Physicists dream of a theory connecting such disparate forces as gravity and electromagnetism.

satPassage: The museum's new exhibit brings together objects that seem to have nothing in common: a Viking sword, a Japanese tea bowl, and a nineteenth-century telescope. The curator argues that these ____ artifacts share a hidden theme of craftsmanship passed between generations.

primarySense: dependent on something else happening or being true
otherSenses: (noun) a group of people forming part of a larger group

nearSynonyms.difference: very close; contingent is more formal
based on random choice, not dependent on conditions

examples.text: The job offer is contingent on a background check; if it fails, the offer will be withdrawn.
The mission's launch date is contingent on the weather, since high winds would endanger the rocket.
French support for the Americans was contingent upon proof that they could win a major battle on their own.

satPassage: The city has approved the new stadium, but construction cannot begin until two conditions are met: the team must secure private investors, and an environmental review must find no serious risks. Approval is therefore ____ on both outcomes.

primarySense: existing as a natural, permanent, or essential part of something
etymologyNote: Latin inhaerere 'to stick in, cling to'

nearSynonyms.difference: nearly identical; intrinsic often describes value or worth
the opposite: gained from outside

examples.text: Some risk is inherent in any surgery, no matter how skilled the surgeon or modern the hospital.
Critics argue the voting system is inherently unfair, since its rules favor large parties by design.
The tension inherent in the sonnet form—fourteen lines, strict rhyme—forces poets to compress their ideas.

satPassage: Engineers emphasize that no bridge can be made perfectly safe. Some degree of risk is ____ in any large structure exposed to wind, weather, and heavy traffic; the goal is to reduce that risk to an acceptable level, not to eliminate it.

primarySense: belonging naturally to something; essential to its nature

nearSynonyms.difference: nearly identical; inherent is common with risks and flaws
the opposite: coming from outside

examples.text: Students with intrinsic motivation study because they love the subject, not because of grades or rewards.
Paper money has no intrinsic value; unlike gold coins, it is worth something only because people agree it is.
A star's color is linked to its intrinsic temperature, not to how far it is from Earth.

satPassage: A diamond's high price is often assumed to reflect its natural rarity. Economists point out, however, that diamonds are not especially scarce; their value comes largely from marketing and controlled supply rather than from any ____ quality of the stone itself.

primarySense: present or found everywhere

nearSynonyms.difference: frequent, but not necessarily everywhere
applies to all; ubiquitous stresses being seen everywhere

examples.text: Smartphones became ubiquitous within a decade; today it is hard to find a teenager without one.
Microplastics are now ubiquitous, found in deep ocean trenches, mountain snow, and human blood.
By the 1800s, portraits of the queen were ubiquitous, hanging in schools, post offices, and homes across the empire.

satPassage: Just thirty years ago, coffee shops were rare in many American towns. Today they appear on nearly every street corner, in airports, hospitals, and bookstores—so ____ that it is difficult to imagine a city without them.

primarySense: seemingly contradictory, yet possibly true

nearSynonyms.difference: actually inconsistent; paradoxical only seems so
opposite of what's expected, often with humor

examples.text: Paradoxically, offering more choices can make shoppers less likely to buy anything at all.
The drug has a paradoxical effect in some children: a stimulant that actually calms them down.
Orwell's paradoxical slogan 'War is peace' captures how the regime twists language against itself.

satPassage: It seems contradictory, but studies show that adding a new road to a congested network can actually make overall traffic slower. This ____ result, first described by the mathematician Dietrich Braess, occurs because drivers each choose the route that seems fastest for themselves.

primarySense: open to more than one interpretation; unclear
etymologyNote: Latin ambiguus 'doubtful, going both ways' (ambi- + agere)

nearSynonyms.difference: describes mixed feelings in a person, not unclear meaning
lacking detail; ambiguous has two or more possible meanings

confusables.note: a sentence is ambiguous; a person is ambivalent

examples.text: The novel's ending is ambiguous: readers still argue about whether the hero survives the fall.
The treaty's wording was ambiguous, allowing both nations to claim the disputed river as their border.
The test results were ambiguous, consistent with either infection or a harmless allergy, so doctors ordered another.

satPassage: The final line of the poem—"And then the door was open"—can be read in two ways: as a sign of escape and freedom, or as a sign that danger has finally entered the house. Critics believe the poet left this line deliberately ____.

primarySense: stated clearly and directly, leaving no room for doubt

nearSynonyms.difference: the opposite: suggested but not stated
describes an honest person; explicit describes clear wording

examples.text: The rules were explicit: any student caught using a phone during the exam would receive a zero.
The Constitution does not make explicit the right to privacy, so courts have inferred it from other clauses.
Rather than hinting, the author makes the theme explicit in the final line: 'Greed ruins everything it touches.'

satPassage: Earlier versions of the policy merely suggested that employees should avoid sharing passwords. The revised policy leaves nothing to interpretation: it ____ forbids password sharing and lists the penalties for violations.

primarySense: suggested or understood without being directly stated
etymologyNote: Latin implicitus 'entangled, folded in' (in- + plicare 'to fold')

nearSynonyms.difference: the opposite: stated outright
naturally part of something, not merely suggested

examples.text: Though the story never says so, there is an implicit criticism of the war in every scene of empty homes.
The ad's implicit message was that buying the car would make you more attractive, though it never said so.
Implicit in the experiment's design was the assumption that all the mice responded to light in the same way.

satPassage: The mayor never directly criticized the previous administration in her speech. Yet when she promised "a government that finally answers its phones," her disapproval was ____, and many listeners understood exactly whom she meant.

primarySense: logically connected and consistent; easy to follow

nearSynonyms.difference: about parts sticking together as a group; coherent is about logic
beautifully expressed, not just logical

examples.text: The government lacked a coherent plan, announcing one policy on Monday and reversing it on Friday.
Her editor helped turn a pile of scattered notes into a coherent story with a clear beginning and end.
Newton's laws offered a coherent explanation for both falling apples and orbiting moons.

satPassage: The first draft of the report was a collection of unrelated observations with no clear structure. After months of revision, the team organized these findings around a single argument, producing a ____ document in which each section built logically on the last.

primarySense: new and original, unlike anything seen before

nearSynonyms.difference: never happened before, often on a large scale; novel stresses originality
simply recent; novel implies fresh and unusual

examples.text: The team took a novel approach to cleaning oil spills: using hair clippings, which absorb oil surprisingly well.
Paying people to recycle was a novel idea in 1980, but such programs are now common.
The printing press made a novel experience possible: ordinary people reading the same text at the same time in different cities.

satPassage: Most attempts to fight the crop disease relied on chemical sprays. The research team tried something entirely different: they introduced a harmless fungus that outcompetes the harmful one, a ____ strategy that no one had tested before.

primarySense: based on what is generally done or believed; traditional

nearSynonyms.difference: conforming to established doctrine, often religious
frequent; conventional implies accepted custom

examples.text: Conventional wisdom held that ulcers were caused by stress, until two doctors proved bacteria were responsible.
Rejecting conventional storytelling, the author told the tale backward, beginning with the hero's death.
Electric cars still cost more upfront than conventional gasoline cars, though they are cheaper to run.

satPassage: Most nineteenth-century novels followed a familiar pattern, describing events in order from a single narrator's perspective. Virginia Woolf broke sharply with these ____ techniques, shifting between characters' thoughts mid-sentence and abandoning straightforward chronology.

primarySense: never done or known before

nearSynonyms.difference: new and original; unprecedented stresses no prior example at all
rare, but it may have happened before

examples.text: Franklin Roosevelt won an unprecedented fourth term, a feat no president before him had achieved.
The heat wave reached unprecedented temperatures, breaking records that had stood since measurements began.
The pandemic caused an unprecedented shift to remote work; nothing similar had happened in modern history.

satPassage: No country had ever attempted to vaccinate its entire population against a disease within a single year. When the campaign began in 2021, it was an effort ____ in public health history, requiring new systems for manufacturing, shipping, and storing doses.

primarySense: based on random choice or personal whim, not reason
etymologyNote: Latin arbiter 'judge' — left to a judge's discretion

nearSynonyms.difference: by chance with no pattern; arbitrary implies someone's whim
depends on conditions, the opposite of whim

examples.text: Colonial borders were often arbitrary, drawn with a ruler across maps without regard for the peoples living there.
Employees complained that promotions seemed arbitrary, with no clear connection to performance.
The choice of zero on the Celsius scale is not arbitrary; it marks the freezing point of water.

satPassage: Players complained that the referee's calls followed no consistent pattern: identical fouls were punished in one half and ignored in the next. Such ____ decisions, they argued, made it impossible to know which rules the game was actually being played by.

primarySense: out of place; not fitting with its surroundings

nearSynonyms.difference: deviates from a pattern; incongruous clashes with its setting
seemingly contradictory but true

examples.text: The cheerful music was incongruous with the funeral scene, making the moment unsettling rather than sad.
A glass skyscraper rising among medieval churches struck many visitors as incongruous.
Finding tropical plant fossils in Antarctica seemed incongruous until scientists realized the continent once lay near the equator.

satPassage: The director's film is set in a gloomy, rain-soaked city, yet its soundtrack features bright, bouncy pop songs. Some critics found this pairing ____ and distracting, while others argued the clash between image and music was the film's most original feature.

primarySense: including all or nearly all elements; complete in scope

nearSynonyms.difference: careful and strict in method; comprehensive covers everything
the opposite: hasty and partial

examples.text: The comprehensive study examined every published trial—over three hundred—before reaching its conclusion.
Rather than fixing one road at a time, the city adopted a comprehensive transportation plan covering buses, bikes, and highways.
Her comprehensive history of the war covers not only battles but also farming, medicine, and family life.

satPassage: Earlier guides to the region's birds covered only the most common species. The new field guide is far more ____, describing all 612 species recorded in the area, including rare visitors seen only once or twice.

primarySense: individually separate and distinct

nearSynonyms.difference: fundamentally different; discrete just means separate
careful and tactful; a different word entirely

confusables.note: discreet = careful not to attract attention or reveal secrets

examples.text: Energy comes in discrete packets called quanta, rather than flowing as a smooth, continuous stream.
The training is divided into five discrete modules, each of which can be completed separately.
Historians once treated the Renaissance as a discrete period, sharply separated from the Middle Ages, but the change was gradual.

satPassage: Children do not experience language as a string of separate words; they hear a continuous stream of sound. Learning to speak therefore requires them to break that stream into ____ units, figuring out where one word ends and the next begins.

primarySense: given or felt by each side toward the other; mutual

nearSynonyms.difference: shared equally; reciprocal stresses exchange in return
similar, not exchanged

examples.text: The two countries signed a reciprocal agreement: each would drop visa requirements for the other's citizens.
Bees and flowers share a reciprocal relationship—the flower provides nectar and the bee carries its pollen.
Their admiration was reciprocal; each poet dedicated a book to the other.

satPassage: Cleaner fish remove parasites from the mouths of larger fish, which in turn refrain from eating them. Because each species benefits from the other, biologists describe this arrangement as ____ rather than one-sided.

primarySense: of minor importance; at the edge rather than the center

nearSynonyms.difference: small in effect; peripheral is about position or relevance
the opposite: most noticeable and important

examples.text: The debate wasted an hour on peripheral issues and never reached the central question of funding.
Owls have poor peripheral vision, so they turn their heads almost completely around to see behind them.
The maid, a peripheral character in the first act, becomes the hero by the play's end.

satPassage: The documentary devotes most of its runtime to minor details—the scientists' favorite meals, the weather during their trip—while barely mentioning the discovery itself. Critics argued that by focusing on such ____ matters, the film missed its own central story.

primarySense: most noticeable or important; standing out
etymologyNote: Latin salire 'to leap' — leaping out at you

nearSynonyms.difference: clearly stated; salient is prominent
the opposite: at the edge, minor

examples.text: The report's salient finding was clear: children who ate breakfast scored higher on every test.
The most salient feature of her poetry is its silence—lines broken by long white gaps.
The lawyer summarized the salient facts of the case in two minutes, ignoring dozens of minor details.

satPassage: The study collected data on dozens of factors, from diet to sleep to screen time. Its most ____ result, however, stood out above all the others: students who exercised for twenty minutes before class scored substantially higher on memory tests.
mnemonic: SALIENT ~ 'leaping' (salire): the fact that leaps off the page.

primarySense: showing subtle differences or shades of meaning

nearSynonyms.difference: has many parts; nuanced stresses fine distinctions
unclear in meaning; nuanced is precise about subtleties

examples.text: Her nuanced account of Columbus shows him neither as hero nor villain but as a man with real achievements and real crimes.
The actor gave a nuanced performance, letting small changes in his voice reveal the villain's hidden grief.
The latest research offers a more nuanced picture of fat: some kinds harm the heart, while others protect it.

satPassage: Earlier biographies portrayed the inventor as either a selfless genius or a ruthless thief of other people's ideas. The new biography rejects both extremes, offering a ____ portrait that acknowledges his brilliance while documenting the credit he unfairly denied his assistants.

primarySense: of the same kind throughout; uniform

nearSynonyms.difference: comparable across two things; homogeneous is uniform within one
exactly the same; homogeneous means consistent in makeup

examples.text: Salt water is a homogeneous mixture: once stirred, every drop contains the same proportion of salt.
The study's sample was too homogeneous—nearly all participants were college students of the same age—to generalize from.
The village was once ethnically homogeneous, but a century of immigration transformed it into one of the most diverse towns in the country.

satPassage: Researchers worried that their results might not apply to the wider population. All of their participants were male graduate students between the ages of 22 and 26, a sample so ____ that it captured almost none of the variety found in society.
mnemonic: HOMO (same) + GEN (kind): all the same kind.

primarySense: deviating from what is standard, normal, or expected

nearSynonyms.difference: clashes with its setting; anomalous breaks a pattern
never happened before; anomalous deviates from a norm

examples.text: Mercury's orbit was anomalous, drifting in a way Newton's laws could not explain until Einstein's theory did.
One school's scores were anomalous—far higher than its neighbors'—which prompted an investigation into cheating.
The warm winter of 1709 was not typical; it was an anomalous break in a century of bitter cold.

satPassage: Across forty years of measurements, the lake's temperature followed a steady seasonal pattern. The 2016 readings broke sharply from that pattern, showing midwinter water warmer than most summers—data so ____ that researchers first assumed their instruments were faulty.
